explanation: Fires on many unrelated tokens: often a middle or later subword piece of a technical or rare word (fib|rosis, neoant|ig|ens, sc|int|igraphy, counter|f|actuals, transce|ivers), and also on '(AP)' datelines, 'decoder', 'which of the following', and baseball 'ERA'. These share no clear theme, so it is hard to predict.

Fires on function words that open a noun phrase, mostly 'the', 'a', 'an' and 'of' right after a verb or preposition ('one of the', 'set of', 'lock the', 'Moreover, the'). It also fires on the first digit of a number after '$' or '='. Content words get little.

Fires on a middle subword piece inside a long, Latinate, multi-token word, especially before a suffix like -ically, -able or -ance (intr|ins|ically, irreconc|il|able, ab|omin|able, syn|cret|ic, ag|glomer|ates). It is weaker on the first piece of such words and silent on whole common words.

Fires on acronyms or abbreviations right after an opening parenthesis, where the acronym defines the spelled-out term just before it ('randomized controlled trials (RCT)', '(PEG)', '(CT)', '(NK)'). This includes later letters of the acronym and the closing paren. It is weaker on variable or symbol names in equations, and code identifiers get little.

Fires on tokens in boilerplate headers, especially source-file license and copyright preambles ('namespace' or 'package' after the license comment, 'www' in apache.org URLs, 'Code generated by', 'GNU') and the '0' in paper section anchors like '{#sec001}'. It also fires on 'has been' in abstracts and on digits inside years and numbers. Overall it is a mix tied to formulaic text and digits.

Fires on a coordinator or punctuation that ends one clause or list item and leads into the next: 'and', 'as well (as)', commas, periods, '?' plus newline, '!!!', '…'. It is strongest after a long noun phrase, where the sentence continues with another item or clause.

Fires on tokens inside software license and copyright header comments ('released under the MIT License', 'See License.txt in the project root for license information', 'distributed with this source code', 'Permission is hereby granted,'). It is weaker on similar legal or disclaimer boilerplate elsewhere and silent in ordinary prose.

Fires on the later token of a multi-token proper name, mostly names of sports teams, organizations, schools or places ('Kansas City Athletics', 'UNC Pembroke', 'Merthyr', 'Kappa Delta Rho', 'NCAA Division', 'Southwest Atlanta Christian'). It is strongest in sports or institutional contexts and weak on generic nouns.

Fires mostly on legal and court-document formatting tokens (the 'BY:' after ATTORNEY GENERAL, 'MEMORANDUM BY', party names in capitals like IMMIGRATION, 'filed ... by', 'IN WITNESS WHEREOF ... set'). It also fires on email header fields ('From:') and on some networking or code tokens (tcphdr, bind). This is a loose mix of legal and administrative text.

No coherent pattern. It fires on varied tokens: 'time stamp' in an archived-article notice, 'methanol' in chemistry, 'To:' in email headers, 'author' in code docs, 'Super Bowl', 'CI' after 95%, 'the benefit of priority', 'my desk'.

Fires on a token that follows an operator or opening delimiter in math or technical text, especially the first number after ' - ' or ' = ' in algebra problems, and on acronyms after '('. It also fires on scattered prose words (soft, special, situation), so it is a partial mixture.

Fires on tokens in non-English text (French, Portuguese, Italian) and in foreign or unusual names (Shkodran, Nasr ibn Sayyar, McLaughlin). It also fires on digits inside model or gene identifiers and version strings (BMP180, p16, Python 3.6). Often the token is a word or name piece in an unfamiliar context, but the set is mixed.

No clear unifying feature. It fires on scattered tokens: the noun modifier in compounds ('science fiction', 'heat-resistant', 'self-care', 'medical conditions'), decimal points in percentages, '=' in tuple unpacking, conjunctions in names ('Northern and Southern', 'ELECTRIC & POWER').

Fires on anatomical location words in medical or biological text: the modifier or determiner just before an anatomical structure name ('dorsal root', 'neural tube', 'the left abducens nerve', 'medial prefrontal', 'right ventricle') and adjectival suffixes like -al in 'popliteal' or 'duodenal'. It is weak outside anatomy.

Fires on the name being declared at the start of a code statement or parameter list: the variable on the left of an assignment ('log = ...', 'window = ...', 'const response'), or a function's first parameter ('function(event', 'extractData(res'). It is strongest at the start of a new line in code.

Fires on distributive quantifiers, mainly 'each' or 'Each', plus 'every' and foreign equivalents (Danish 'hver', French 'chaque'). It is moderate on 'per' and on 'of' in 'each of', and weak on 'everyone' or 'daily'.

The strongest cue is 'See' or 'see' as a cross-reference instruction ('See also', 'Please see our Privacy Notice', 'See the ...'). The rest is a diverse mix (Karnofsky, '(' after a name, commas after dates, 'this caliber'), so it is not cleanly predictable.

Fires on subword tokens in foreign-language text (Danish, Finnish, Greek, Portuguese, Italian, German, Chinese bytes) and on verb or conjunction tokens in software license boilerplate ('and is licensed under', 'are unable to', 'for license information'). It also fires on Latin 'summa cum laude'. Two or more unrelated groups.

Fires on tokens spelled with 'cast', 'coast', 'cust' or 'const' (Cast, CASTILLO, coast, Coastal, custards, Custard, constellations, const, Belcastro), whatever the meaning. It is weakly active on compass words like North and South near place names.

Fires on the first piece of a word split into several subword tokens, often in foreign-language text (Spanish, French, German, Maori) or scientific names ('circ|ov|irus', 'D|rosophila', 'd|engue', 'hant|av|iruses'). There are also scattered hits (commas, 'et al.'), so the pattern is diffuse.

Fires on a word-initial fragment token, especially 'st' at the start of a word split into pieces ('st|enosis', 'st|ents', 'st|unts', 'st|abilities', 'st|ably'). It also fires on similar opening fragments in French and Norwegian ('impr', 'sup', 'conf', 'ent'). It is weak on whole words.
